title: Shame
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino contrasts two scenes: a teacher visibly cringing when a colleague misapplies dual coding as 'visual learning,' and the same teacher patiently, non-judgmentally correcting a student's misconception that deoxygenated blood is blue. She uses the pairing to argue that staffrooms extend far less grace to adult misconceptions than classrooms extend to student ones, even though a colleague's misconception (like conflating learning styles with dual coding) may shape far more student learning than any individual student error. Castelino attributes the colleague's mistaken belief to thin, unfollowed-up CPD rather than to a lack of intelligence or effort, since most teachers simply don't have time to read the underlying research themselves and are left with surface-level, easily-muddled versions of what they were taught. She's explicit that she's been both figures, sometimes confidently wrong after a shallow CPD session, sometimes judgmental of colleagues holding views she herself used to hold, and frames the piece as a call to replace staffroom shaming with the same open, patient stance teachers already extend to students, since shame discourages the very willingness to update one's views that good practice requires.
points: Castelino's core comparison, cringing at a colleague's misconception versus patiently correcting a student's, exposes an asymmetry in how much grace staffrooms extend to adult versus child error.

She attributes colleagues' persistent misconceptions (like conflating dual coding with visual learning styles) to thin, unfollowed-up CPD rather than to intelligence or effort, since few teachers have time to read primary research themselves.

She explicitly implicates herself on both sides of the dynamic, having been both the confidently-wrong colleague and the judgmental one, which grounds the argument in self-critique rather than pure external criticism.

Her practical call to action is to replace staffroom shaming with the same patient, understanding stance already extended to students, arguing shame actively discourages the willingness to update views.
quotes: Ms C cringes visibly. Now, most of us have heard about how learning styles are a myth and not useful when thinking of learning in the classroom.
With Ms J, she could not hide her disdain but with her students, there was more understanding.
It is highly likely she was told about learning styles and dual coding in a CPD session with very little in terms of a follow-up or reflection.
I am not trying to make Ms J out to be someone who isn’t intelligent enough or resourceful. I have been a version of Ms J.
But I have also been a version of Ms C and been judgemental of others who still hold views I used to and that I feel have been proven wrong.
We need to stop shaming those we perceive to believe the ‘wrong’ things. And we need to stop feeling ashamed if we need to change our views and learn.
